卡沙卡是一種源自西非的傳統打擊樂器，由兩個裝有豆類的小葫蘆組成，透過繩子連接。演: The kashaka is a traditional percussion instrument from West Africa, made of two small gourds filled with beans and joined by a string. The player holds one gourd and the other swings quickly around the hand, clicking when it strikes. Simple and easy to use, it plays an important part in the traditional music of West African peoples, and is often heard at rituals and celebrations. As African culture spread around the world and across the Atlantic, the kashaka travelled too and was reinterpreted and renamed in different cultures. In Japan it is called patica and in the United States koshika, and elsewhere there are other names such as asalato and keskes. This reflects the way instruments mix and change as they globalise, and has made it a representative instrument of modern world music, both local and international.
卡沙卡是一種簡單的打擊樂器，由兩個裝有豆類的小葫蘆組成（本質上是由繩子連接的兩個: The kashaka is a simple percussion instrument made of two small gourds filled with beans, in effect two small shakers joined by a string. One gourd is held in the hand and the other swings quickly from side to side around it, clicking when they strike. It comes from West Africa but has reappeared under different names in many countries: patica in Japan, koshika in the United States. Other names include asalato, keskes, tchangotche and koshka.
卡沙卡的音色明亮而清脆，具有節奏感強烈的打擊特徵。其音質乾爽有力，帶有輕快的「咔: The kashaka's timbre is bright and crisp, with a strongly rhythmic percussion character. The sound is dry and forceful, a light clicking, and the range sits in the middle and upper register. It sounds when the two bean-filled gourds strike each other; the resonance is simple and direct, relying on the cavity of the gourds and the physical vibration of the beans. Compared with the soft rustle of a maraca it carries better; compared with the metallic quality of a tambourine it is warmer and more natural. The sound has a raw, plain character and a clearly defined rhythmic outline, and suits the atmosphere of African folk music particularly well, while giving modern music a distinctive percussion layer and local colour.
卡沙卡連珠搖響器的發聲體為兩個空心葫蘆，內部裝入豆子；傳統做法亦以薩赫勒鐵質土壤: The kashaka's sounding body is two hollow gourds filled with beans; traditionally they are also filled with orange pebbles from the iron-bearing soils of the Sahel, and on the West African coast with fragments of shell. The two gourds are joined by a short cord, sometimes braided from strips of old cloth. Making one also uses a stick, glue and a saw: a knot is tied in the cord, which is threaded through the hole in the gourd, a stick is pressed against the thin wall and glued in place, and the protruding part is sawn off. Another method makes the cord length adjustable by drilling both gourds and knotting the cord through. The materials of the other parts are not stated in the source.

演奏時一手握住其中一個葫蘆，另一手將相連的葫蘆快速左右甩動，使其繞手回擺並互相撞: Hold one gourd in one hand and swing the joined gourd quickly from side to side with the other, so that it swings back around the hand and the two strike each other, making both a rattle and a knock. Beginners first practise catching the gourd they have swung, because only once you can catch it reliably can you vary the rhythm. Hands differ in size, so choose a kashaka that fits; if the cord length is adjustable, set it so that it is easy to control. Once that is secure you can hold one in each hand and play different time signatures against each other, making polyrhythm.
